beats.say: FastAPI, topic by topic. Like the Python lecture, this one follows the FastAPI page exactly: the same ten modules, in the same order, and in each module, the same questions with the same numbers. Each module starts with the idea as a picture, then the questions, then a check.
Here's what gets asked most, from the same four hundred and fifty six interview write-ups. By far the most common: what is FastAPI, and why is it popular. Twelve write-ups.
Dependency injection, four.
Middleware, four.
JWT authentication, four.
Rate limiting, caching and pagination, three.
So the opening question deserves a really good answer, and that's where we start.
Module one. FastAPI foundations. What FastAPI is, what it's built on, how it runs, and how it compares with Flask and Django.
Here's the idea of the whole framework, as layers. A request first reaches Uvicorn, which is an ASGI server. It deals with sockets and HTTP, and then calls your application.
Underneath FastAPI is Starlette, a lightweight web toolkit. Routing, requests and responses, middleware, WebSockets and streaming all come from Starlette.
FastAPI's own contribution is reading your function signatures. It looks at the type hints, and Pydantic validates and converts the incoming data to match them.
So by the time your function runs, it receives clean, typed values. You write a normal Python function. The framework handles the HTTP, the checking, and the documentation.
Question one, asked in twelve write-ups. What is FastAPI, and why is it popular?
Say what it's built on, the one central idea, and then a few concrete reasons, in that order.
The central idea: you write normal Python type hints, and FastAPI uses them for everything. Here's a Pydantic model for the request body.

And one route. From this signature alone, FastAPI knows space id comes from the path and must be an int, the body must match Question, and debug is an optional query parameter. It validates all of it, converts the types, returns a clear 422 error if anything is wrong, serialises the response, and documents it all in interactive docs at slash docs. One declaration, five things for free.
Here's the answer, to say out loud.
FastAPI is a modern Python framework for building APIs, built on Starlette for the web layer, which is ASGI, and Pydantic for data.
Its central idea is that type hints drive everything: validation, conversion, serialisation and documentation. So there's less code, and fewer bugs.
It's async-first, so one process handles many concurrent requests that are waiting on I/O, like database or LLM calls.
It generates OpenAPI docs automatically, at slash docs, and it has a clean dependency injection system.
So it's fast to write and fast to run, which is why it's become the default for Python APIs, and especially for ML and LLM services.
Question two. What's the difference between WSGI and ASGI?
Both are contracts between a server and a Python app. The difference is what a worker can do while a request waits.

WSGI, the classic interface used by Flask and Django, is synchronous. A worker takes one request and is tied up until it finishes, waiting included. To serve more at once, you add more threads or processes.
ASGI is the asynchronous successor. One worker runs an event loop, so while one request waits on the database, the same worker serves others.

And ASGI isn't only about speed. It also supports WebSockets, streaming responses, and lifespan events: connections that outlive a single request, which WSGI simply can't express. That's why FastAPI is built on ASGI.
Question three. What are Uvicorn and Gunicorn, and how do you run FastAPI in production?
What each one does, and how you get more than one CPU core working.
Uvicorn is the ASGI server. It accepts connections and runs your app. Each Uvicorn process runs one event loop, and so uses one CPU core.

To use more cores on one machine, you run several worker processes. Gunicorn is a mature process manager that does that: it starts the workers, restarts any that crash, and handles graceful reloads. Uvicorn also has a workers flag of its own now.

In containers, the usual choice is simpler: one Uvicorn process per container, and the platform, like Kubernetes, scales the number of replicas. Either way, behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that handles TLS.
Question four, asked in four write-ups. How does FastAPI compare with Flask and Django?
Compare honestly, and finish with when you'd choose each one. Interviewers like hearing that the others still have their place.
FastAPI is API-first and driven by type hints. It's async-first on ASGI, and validation and docs are built in. But it doesn't bring an ORM, an admin panel, or user management: you pick those.
Flask is a minimal micro-framework. Synchronous at heart, with extensions for everything, and lots of freedom. Great for small and simple apps.
Django is batteries included: an ORM, migrations, an admin site, authentication, templates. With Django REST Framework for APIs, and async support that's growing.
So: for APIs and ML or LLM services, FastAPI. For a small, simple app, Flask is fine. For a full product with a database at its centre and an admin site, Django is very hard to beat.
Check 1. Your FastAPI app runs as one Uvicorn process on an eight core VM, and CPU sits at twelve percent. Why, and what do you change?

One Uvicorn process runs one event loop, which uses one core, and one core out of eight is about twelve percent. Run several workers, with Gunicorn or the workers flag, or more replicas in containers.
Module two. Requests and responses. How FastAPI decides where each parameter comes from, what it does with what you return, and the details of status codes, headers and files.
Here's the idea: one request's trip through FastAPI. First, the route is matched by its method and path.
Then every parameter is extracted from the right place: the path, the query string, the JSON body, headers or cookies.
Everything is converted to its declared type and validated. If anything is wrong, the client gets a 422, and your function never runs.
Your function runs with clean values, and returns a dict, a Pydantic model, or a Response object.
And on the way out, the return value is filtered through the response model and serialised to JSON. Five stages. Most questions in this module are about one of them.
Question five. How do path parameters, query parameters and the request body work?
The rule FastAPI follows to decide where each parameter comes from.

FastAPI decides where each parameter comes from by how you declare it. A name that appears in the path string, in curly braces, is a path parameter. Here, user id, converted to an int: send abc, and you get a 422.
A plain type that's not in the path, like a str, int or bool, is a query parameter. Give it a default, and it's optional. Query lets you add constraints, like a maximum of a hundred.
And a Pydantic model is the JSON request body. For anything else, you say so explicitly, with Header, Cookie, Form or File.
Question six. What is response model, and why use it?
What it does to your return value, and the security reason it matters.
Response model, or simply the return type annotation, tells FastAPI the shape of the response. Separate models for input and output is the usual pattern: User In has a password; User Out doesn't.

Then even if the function returns the full database object, with the password hash and internal flags, only the fields in User Out are sent. That's the security reason: it stops you leaking internal fields by accident. It also validates the output, and documents it in the OpenAPI schema.
Question seven. How do you set status codes and return different kinds of responses?
The default, how to change it, and the Response classes, with one catch.
By default, whatever you return becomes JSON with status 200. Status code on the decorator changes the default, like 201 for created, or 202 for accepted.
For errors, raise HTTPException with the status and a detail message. It stops the function and becomes a JSON error response.

And you can return a Response class directly: JSONResponse, StreamingResponse, FileResponse, HTML or redirects. The catch: a Response returned directly skips response model validation, so you're responsible for what's in it.
Question eight. How do you handle headers, cookies, forms and file uploads?
The markers to use, and the right way to accept a file.

Headers, cookies and form fields are declared with Header, Cookie and Form. Header converts underscores to hyphens, so user agent reads the User Agent header. Forms and files need the python multipart package installed.

For files, use UploadFile, not bytes. UploadFile is a spooled temporary file: kept in memory up to a size, then moved to disk, with async read. Read it in chunks for big files. Bytes would load the whole thing into memory. And validate the size and type before you trust it.
Check 2. A route at slash tenant slash search has a function with tenant, a string, q, a string, and page, an int with default one. Where does each come from?

Tenant is in the path string, so it's a path parameter. Q is a plain type not in the path, with no default, so it's a required query parameter. And page is an optional query parameter, with a default of one.
Module three. Pydantic models in FastAPI. What happens when data is wrong, what changed in Pydantic two, and typed configuration.
Here's the idea of this module. A request arrives with an empty text and a top k of the word many.

FastAPI validates before calling your function, finds both problems, and replies 422, Unprocessable Entity, listing every error with its location and a message. Your function never ran. So inside your function, you can trust the data completely.
Question nine. How does FastAPI use Pydantic for validation, and what happens when validation fails?
When validation happens, what the error looks like, and how you'd customise it.
Every typed parameter and every model is validated and converted before your function runs. Field adds constraints: lengths, ranges. Literal limits a value to a fixed set.
A field validator adds your own rule, and can also clean the value, like stripping whitespace.
If anything fails, FastAPI raises a request validation error and returns 422 with the details. To match your company's error format, register an exception handler for request validation error.
Question ten. What changed between Pydantic version one and version two?
The speed, and the renames you'll meet in real code.
Version one used dot dict and dot json, parse obj, the validator decorators, and an inner Config class with orm mode.
Version two renamed them: model dump and model dump json, model validate and model validate json, field validator and model validator, and model config with from attributes.
And the big change underneath: version two's core was rewritten in Rust, so validation is several times, up to tens of times, faster. Current FastAPI requires version two.
Question eleven. How do you manage configuration with pydantic settings?
Typed config that fails at startup, and how to hand it out.

Pydantic settings loads typed, validated configuration from environment variables and dot env files. A required field with no default means a missing variable fails at startup, not on the first request that needs it. Secret str hides keys in logs.
Wrap it in a cached function, so it's read once.
And hand it out with Depends rather than a global import. That way, tests can override the settings with dependency overrides. Which is exactly the next module.
Check 3. A request has an invalid body. Does any line of your route function run before the 422 is returned?
No. Validation happens before your function is called, so the 422 comes straight from FastAPI, and none of your code runs.
Module four. Dependency injection, with Depends. Asked in four write-ups, and it's the feature that makes FastAPI apps testable.
Here's the idea. A route doesn't build what it needs. It declares it. Ask needs a user and a database session.
FastAPI calls those dependencies for you, before the route runs. Get current user, and get db.
And dependencies can declare dependencies of their own. The user needs the bearer token, and the db needs the settings. So they form a tree, and FastAPI resolves it, from the leaves up.
Notice that both the route and get current user need get db. Within one request, FastAPI calls it once and shares the result, so they use the same session. That's per-request caching.
Question twelve, asked in four write-ups. How does dependency injection work in FastAPI?
What a dependency is, how they chain, and the three reasons to use them.

A dependency is just a function, or a class, that FastAPI calls before the route, injecting what it returns. It can declare parameters exactly like a route: query parameters, headers, or other dependencies. And it can raise HTTPException to stop the request, like a 401 here.
The route asks for the user with Depends. If the dependency raises, the route never runs.
And you can attach dependencies to a whole router, or the whole app, for checks like an API key on every route.
Said out loud.
A dependency is a function or class that FastAPI calls before the route, and injects its return value.
Dependencies can depend on other dependencies. FastAPI resolves the whole tree, and calls each one once per request.
A dependency that yields gets setup and teardown, which is how you manage a database session.
I use them for authentication, database sessions, settings, shared clients and permission checks: declared once, reused everywhere.
And they make the app testable, because dependency overrides can swap any of them for a fake.
Question thirteen. What are yield dependencies, and how do you manage a database session with them?
The shape, when each part runs, and the rules for sessions.
A dependency that yields works like a context manager. FastAPI runs it up to the yield. Here, that opens a database session.
The yielded value is injected into the route, which runs.
Once the route is done, FastAPI resumes the dependency after the yield, to clean up: commit, or roll back if something raised, and close the session.
The rule: one session per request, created and closed by a yield dependency. Never a global session shared across requests, because sessions aren't safe to share between concurrent requests.
The engine, with its connection pool, is created once for the app. The session maker produces one session per request.
Get db opens a session, and yields it to the route.
After the route, it commits, or on an exception, rolls back and re-raises. The async with closes the session either way. Exactly the context manager pattern from Python module six.
Question fourteen. How are dependencies cached, and how do you use classes as dependencies?
The per-request cache, how to turn it off, and parameterised dependencies with classes.

Within one request, if several dependencies use the same function, FastAPI calls it once and reuses the result. That's why the route and the user lookup share one session. Pass use cache equals false to get a fresh call.
A class can be a dependency too. A class with dunder call is perfect for a configurable dependency: the constructor takes the settings, like ten per minute, and call runs on each request.
So Depends of RateLimiter of ten gives you a rate limit you can tune per route. Remember the instance is created once, when the app starts; dunder call runs per request.
Question fifteen. How do you override dependencies in tests?
One dictionary, and why it's the main reason to route things through Depends.
A fake LLM client: same method, canned answer. No network, no cost, and a predictable result.
App dot dependency overrides maps the real dependency function to a replacement. Every route that depends on get llm now gets the fake, and the user lookup returns a test user.

Then call the route with the test client, assert, and clear the overrides. This is the main reason to get everything through Depends: database sessions, settings, auth, and LLM clients all become swappable in tests.
Check 4. The route and get current user both depend on get db. How many database sessions does one request open? A, one. B, two. C, one per query. Or D, none until commit.
A. One. FastAPI caches each dependency's result within a request, so the route and the user lookup share the same session, unless you pass use cache equals false.
Module five. Async in FastAPI. Three questions about the single most common way to make a FastAPI service slow: blocking the event loop.
Here's the idea of this module. Each Uvicorn worker has one event loop. A route defined with async def runs directly on that loop. So it must await its I/O, and never block.
While ask awaits the model's reply, the loop is free to serve the health check, and every other request.

A route defined with plain def is treated differently. FastAPI runs it in a thread pool, forty threads by default, so the blocking code inside it can't freeze the loop. That one difference decides the next three answers.
Question sixteen. What's the difference between async def and def routes in FastAPI?
Where each one runs, and the rule for choosing.

An async def route runs on the event loop. Use it when everything inside is async: an async HTTP client, an async database driver, async Redis. Then one worker can handle thousands of concurrent requests that are waiting. But one blocking call inside it stalls the whole worker.

A def route runs in the thread pool. Use it when you call blocking libraries, like requests, a synchronous database driver, or a synchronous SDK. It's safe, but limited by the pool: with forty threads, the forty first slow request waits for a thread to free up.
So the rule: if the libraries inside are async, async def. If they're blocking, plain def, or await them with to thread. The worst choice is async def with blocking calls inside.
Question seventeen. What happens if you call blocking code inside an async endpoint, and how do you fix it?
What the symptom looks like in production, and the fixes.
Here's an async def route calling a synchronous LLM SDK, which takes three seconds. That call never awaits, so the event loop can't switch to anything else.

So every other request on that worker, even the health check, is stuck for three seconds. In production, the symptom is latency spiking across all endpoints together, and health checks failing under load, even though CPU is low.

The fixes. Use the async version of the client. Or make the route a plain def. Or await asyncio dot to thread on the blocking call. And for heavy CPU work, a process pool, or a job queue with separate workers.
Question eighteen. How do you call external APIs efficiently from FastAPI?
One shared client created at startup, timeouts everywhere, and calls made concurrently but capped.

One shared async client for the whole app, created at startup in the lifespan and closed at shutdown, so connections are pooled and reused. With a timeout on every call, and a limit on connections. Creating a new client per request means a new TCP and TLS handshake every time.

And independent calls run concurrently, with gather or a TaskGroup, capped by a semaphore. Plus retries with backoff on transient errors, and a circuit breaker if a dependency is down, so you fail fast instead of piling up waiting requests.
Check 5. An async def route calls requests dot get. Under load, the health check starts timing out. Why?

Because requests is blocking. Inside async def, it stalls the event loop, so every request on that worker waits, health checks included. Use an async client like httpx, make the route a plain def, or await to thread.
Module six. Application structure and lifecycle. How a bigger app is organised, what happens at startup and shutdown, middleware, and errors.
Here's the idea of the module. An app has a lifecycle. Once, before it serves anything, the lifespan opens database pools, creates shared clients, and loads models.
Then every request passes through layers: middleware, then a router, then the route, which calls a service and a repository.
Routers are how a big app is split up: one per domain, each with its own prefix and dependencies.
And once, on shutdown, the lifespan closes everything gracefully. Lifespan, middleware, routers, errors: the four questions of this module.
Question nineteen, asked in three write-ups. How do you structure a larger FastAPI application?
Routers to split the app, a layout by domain, and layers inside each domain.

Organise by domain: a folder per area, like chat and documents, each with the same shape. A router that does HTTP only: parameters, status codes. A service with the business logic, which doesn't import FastAPI, so it's easy to test. A repository for database queries. And schemas for the Pydantic models. It's the same layering as controller, service, repository in Spring.
Each domain's APIRouter has a prefix, tags for the docs, and shared dependencies, like requiring a logged-in user. Main dot py creates the app with its lifespan, and includes each router.
Question twenty. What are lifespan events, and what should run at startup and shutdown?
The shape, and what belongs in it.

The lifespan is an async context manager around the app's whole life. Code before the yield runs once at startup: connection pools, shared HTTP clients, and anything slow to build, like loading an embedding model. Loading a model per request is a classic mistake.
The app serves requests while the lifespan sits at the yield.
Code after the yield runs at shutdown: close clients and pools. It replaces the old on event startup and shutdown decorators. Store the objects on app dot state, and hand them out with dependencies.
Question twenty one, asked in four write-ups. How does middleware work in FastAPI?
What it wraps, the order layers run in, and when to use a dependency instead.
Middleware wraps every request and response. It runs code before the request reaches the routes, and after the response is produced. And like stacked decorators, the order matters.
Timing was added first, so it sits nearest the routes.
Request id goes around it: it tags each request and response with an id, for the logs.
CORS was added last, so it's the outermost layer, and sees the request first. With add middleware, the last one added is the outermost.

A request goes in through the layers to the route, and the response comes back out in reverse. Use middleware for cross-cutting concerns that apply to everything: logging, timing, request ids, CORS, compression, security headers.
A function middleware receives the request and call next. Await call next to run the rest of the app, then change the response, here adding a timing header.

Middleware versus dependencies. Middleware runs for every request, but it can't see route parameters, and can't use Depends. Dependencies attach to specific routes or routers, are typed, and are easy to override in tests. So authentication and permissions belong in dependencies, and truly global concerns in middleware.
Question twenty two. How do you handle errors in FastAPI?
HTTPException for the simple case, and custom handlers for a clean design.
HTTPException is fine for simple cases in a route. For a clean design, the service layer raises domain errors, like not found or provider busy, without knowing anything about HTTP.
One exception handler turns all of them into a consistent JSON error contract: an error code, a message, and the request id, so support can find it in the logs.
Services stay framework-agnostic and testable. And never return stack traces or SQL errors to clients: log them with the request id, and send a generic 500.
Check 6. Where should a two gigabyte embedding model be loaded in a FastAPI app, and why not in the route?

In the lifespan, once at startup, stored on app dot state and handed out with a dependency. Loading it in the route would reload it on every request, costing seconds of latency and a lot of memory churn.
Check 7. You add middleware A, then middleware B. Which one sees the request first?
B. The last middleware added is the outermost layer, so it sees the request first, and the response last.
Module seven. Security. JWT authentication was asked in four write-ups, and role checks and API keys follow from it.

Here's the idea. The client logs in once, sending a username and password. The server checks the password against its stored hash, and signs a token, a JWT, saying who the user is and when the token expires.
Then every request carries that token, in the Authorization header, as a bearer token.
The server verifies the signature and the expiry, and knows who the user is, without a database lookup for the session. That's what makes JWTs stateless.
Question twenty three, asked in four write-ups. How do you implement JWT authentication in FastAPI?
The code shape, and then the security points, which are what interviewers are listening for.
OAuth2 password bearer reads the bearer token from the Authorization header, and makes the Authorize button work in the docs.
Creating a token: the user id as the subject, a short expiry, signed with a secret.

And the dependency: decode and verify the token, which checks the signature and the expiry, and pin the allowed algorithms. On failure, a 401. On success, load the user. Then any route that needs a user just depends on get current user.
Hash passwords with bcrypt or Argon2, which are slow and salted on purpose. Never store or log a plain password.
Keep access tokens short-lived, minutes, with refresh tokens to get new ones. A JWT can't be revoked before it expires without extra state, like a deny list, so short expiry is your main control.
A JWT is signed, not encrypted. Anyone holding it can read the payload. So never put secrets in it.
And verify properly: pin the algorithm, check expiry, and audience and issuer if you use them. Never accept the algorithm none. And HTTPS everywhere, because a stolen token is a stolen session.
Question twenty four. How do you implement role-based access and API keys?
Both are dependencies. Roles use a factory; API keys use a header scheme.
Role-based access is a dependency factory: a function that takes the allowed roles, and returns a dependency that checks the current user's role. A closure, just like a decorator with arguments.
So a route says depends on require role admin. 401 means we don't know who you are; 403 means we know, and you're not allowed.

API keys, for service-to-service or partner access, use APIKeyHeader. Store only a hash of each key, compare in constant time with secrets dot compare digest, and support rotation. These security classes also show lock icons in the docs.
Check 8. Can you put a user's email and plan inside a JWT payload? What about their password? Why?

The email and plan are fine, as long as it's acceptable for the client to read them. The password, never. A JWT is signed, so it can't be tampered with, but it isn't encrypted, so anyone can decode and read it.
Module eight. Databases. Async SQLAlchemy, and the N plus one problem, which was asked in two write-ups.
Here's the idea. The engine, with its pool of database connections, is created once for the whole app, in the lifespan. Opening a database connection is slow, so they're kept and reused.

Each request gets its own session, from a yield dependency, which borrows a connection from the pool and gives it back at the end. One engine per app, one session per request. Never share a session between requests.
Question twenty five. How do you use SQLAlchemy, async, with FastAPI?
The setup, how queries look, and the two async gotchas.
An async engine with an async driver, like asyncpg, and a pool. The session maker with expire on commit false, so objects stay readable after a commit without another query.

Queries use the two point oh style: build a select, then await db dot execute. And here's the first gotcha: lazy loading doesn't work implicitly in async. Touching chat dot messages later would raise an error called missing greenlet. So load relationships explicitly, with selectinload.
The second gotcha: don't mix in synchronous database calls inside async routes. And use Alembic for migrations, never create all in production.
Question twenty six, asked twice. How do you avoid N plus one queries, and tune database access in FastAPI?
What N plus one looks like, the fix, and a short checklist.
N plus one: one query loads a hundred chats, and then reading each chat's messages fires one more query per chat. A hundred and one round trips, and it gets worse as the data grows.

The fix is eager loading. Selectinload runs one extra query, with an IN list of ids, for all the children: two queries total, which suits one to many. Joinedload does it in a single join, which suits many to one. Then the checklist: indexes on foreign keys and filter columns, checked with explain analyze; select only the columns you need; paginate; and size the pool to what the database can take.
Check 9. A page lists fifty orders, and shows each order's customer name. The logs show fifty one queries. What's happening, and what's the fix?

That's N plus one. One query loads the orders, then each order lazily loads its customer, one query each. Eager load the customer, with joinedload, since it's many to one, and it becomes a single query.
Module nine. Beyond request and response. Background work, streaming, WebSockets, rate limits, and token budgets. This is where GenAI services live, because model calls are slow and expensive.
Here's the idea of this module: pick the tool by how long the work takes. Milliseconds: a normal request and response.
Seconds, and the user should see progress: stream the response, with Server-Sent Events. That's how LLM tokens reach a chat UI.
Small work that can happen after the reply: background tasks.
Minutes, like ingesting a big document: a queue with separate workers. Reply 202 with a job id, and let the client poll or get notified.
And when both sides need to send messages at any time, a WebSocket.
Question twenty seven. What are background tasks, and when should you use Celery or a queue instead?
What background tasks really are, their limits, and when the limits matter.

Background tasks run a function after the response is sent, in the same process. That's all. No retries, no persistence: if the process restarts or crashes, the task is gone. And it uses the API worker's own resources. Good for quick, non-critical follow-ups: sending an email, writing an audit log.

For anything long, heavy, or that must not be lost, like embedding a thousand page document, use a real queue: Celery, RQ, Arq, or a cloud queue. Jobs are stored in a broker, run by separate workers with retries, and scale apart from the API. The API enqueues the job, replies 202 with a job id, and the client polls a status endpoint.
Question twenty eight, asked twice. How do you stream responses? StreamingResponse, Server-Sent Events, and LLM tokens.
The generator, the format, and the two production details everyone forgets.
The browser sends one request. FastAPI calls the model with streaming turned on.
As tokens arrive from the model, FastAPI forwards each one immediately, as a server sent event: a line starting with data, then a blank line.
And a final done event. The whole answer takes just as long, but the user sees the first words in half a second instead of waiting eight. That's why every chat product streams.
StreamingResponse takes an async generator, the async generator from the Python lecture. It loops over the model's stream.
Production detail one: check whether the client disconnected, and stop. Otherwise you keep generating, and paying for, tokens nobody will read.
Each token is yielded in SSE format: data, the JSON, and a blank line. Then a done marker.

Production detail two: proxies like nginx buffer responses by default, which would deliver the whole stream at the end. The X Accel Buffering no header, plus no cache, turn that off. SSE is one-way and runs over plain HTTP, so it's simpler than WebSockets for token streaming.
Question twenty nine. How do WebSockets work in FastAPI?
The endpoint shape, and the scaling problem every interviewer asks about next.
A WebSocket is a persistent, two-way connection: chat, live dashboards, collaborative editing. The endpoint accepts the connection, and registers it.
Then it loops, receiving messages and broadcasting them, until the client disconnects.

The scaling catch: an in-memory connection manager only knows the connections on its own process. With several workers or pods, a message must go through something shared, like Redis pub sub, so every process can deliver it to its own clients. Also: authenticate on connect, and use heartbeats to detect dead connections.
Question thirty, asked in three write-ups. How do you add rate limiting, caching and pagination?
Three separate tools. The common thread: anything shared lives in Redis, not process memory.

Rate limiting: a counter per user, or per key, per time window, stored in Redis. Increment it, set an expiry, and over the limit, reply 429 with a retry after header. A token bucket smooths out bursts. Or do it at the API gateway.
Caching: check the cache, and on a miss, compute and store it with a time to live. The key must include everything that changes the answer, and writes must invalidate it.

Pagination: prefer cursors to offsets. Where id is greater than the last id seen, order by id, limit twenty, uses the index and stays fast. Offset one hundred thousand makes the database scan and throw away a hundred thousand rows.
And the common thread: you run many workers and pods, so a counter or cache in process memory only works for one of them. Anything shared lives in Redis.
Question thirty one. How do you enforce per-user token budgets, and keep the whole service under the LLM provider's rate limit?
Two different limits. One per user, for fairness and cost. One global, for the provider's limit on your key.

Per user: a dependency checks today's token count in Redis before calling the model, and replies 429 when the budget is used up. Limit tokens, not just requests: one request can cost fifty tokens, or fifty thousand.
Globally: a semaphore per process caps the calls in flight. Divide the provider's limit by the number of processes, or use a shared limiter in Redis.

And record the actual usage after the call, because output length is only known at the end. For streaming, record when the stream ends, including when the client disconnects. Status codes: the user's own limit is 429; the provider being saturated is 503, with retry after.
Check 10. Uploading a five hundred page PDF triggers chunking and embedding, about four minutes of work. Background tasks, or a queue?
A queue. It's long, heavy, and must not be lost if the API restarts. Reply 202 with a job id, let separate workers process it with retries, and have the client poll the job's status.
Check 11. Your SSE endpoint works locally, but behind nginx, the whole answer arrives at once, at the end. Why?
Because nginx buffers the response before passing it on. Send the X Accel Buffering no header, with cache control no cache, or turn off proxy buffering for that route.
Module ten. Testing, docs and deployment. The last five questions, ending with the design question that pulls the whole lecture together.
Here's the idea of the last module: what makes a service production-ready. It's tested, with fakes for the slow and expensive parts, and the real thing where it matters.
It's documented, and in FastAPI, the documentation comes from the code itself, so it never drifts.
It's packaged and run well: a slim image, one process per container, and health checks the platform can use.
And it's fast and observable: you can see latency, errors, tokens and cost, per request. One question each, then the design question.
Question thirty two. How do you test FastAPI applications?
The client to use, what to fake, what to keep real, and one trap.

A fixture overrides the edges: the LLM client, payment, email, auth. And creates a TestClient. The trap: use it as a context manager, with with. Only then does the lifespan run, so the startup objects exist.
Test the contract, including the failures: an empty question must give 422, a missing token 401, an unknown id 404.

For async tests, httpx's AsyncClient with an ASGI transport. And keep the core real: a real Postgres in Docker, using Testcontainers, with each test inside a transaction that's rolled back, so tests are fast and isolated.
Question thirty three. How do the automatic API docs work, and how do you customise them?
Where the docs come from, and the knobs.
FastAPI builds an OpenAPI three schema from your routes, type hints, Pydantic models, dependencies and security schemes, served at slash openapi dot json.
On top of it, Swagger UI at slash docs, where you can try requests and authorise with a token, and ReDoc at slash redoc.
You customise it with summaries, descriptions, tags, examples, and documented error responses, and hide internal routes with include in schema false.
And because the schema is standard, you can generate typed client SDKs from it. For a private API, disable or protect the docs in production.
Question thirty four. How do you deploy FastAPI with Docker?
The Dockerfile, then the production checklist.
A slim base image. Copy the dependency files first and install from the lock file, so that layer is cached, and only rebuilds when dependencies change.
Then the code, and run as a non-root user.

One Uvicorn process per container, and scale with replicas. Then the checklist: a liveness endpoint, saying the process is up, and a readiness endpoint, saying the database and Redis are reachable. Graceful shutdown so in-flight requests finish. Config from the environment, secrets from a secret manager, never baked into the image.
Question thirty five. How do you make a FastAPI service fast and observable in production?
Performance habits, then what you measure. For a GenAI service, a few metrics are special.

Fast: async all the way, and never block the loop. One connection pool per database and one shared HTTP client, created at startup. A timeout on every outbound call, because one slow dependency without a timeout can hold every worker. And cache, paginate, and stream.

Observable: latency percentiles per route, p50, p95, p99, and error rates. For an LLM service, also time to first token, tokens in and out, and cost per request. Structured JSON logs carrying a request id. And traces across the API, the vector store and the model, with OpenTelemetry, so you can see where a slow request spent its time. Averages hide pain, so alert on p95.
Question thirty six, the design question. Design the chat endpoint of a GenAI app in FastAPI.
Walk through every layer, in the order a request meets them. Every module of this lecture shows up once.
The route is async def, with a Pydantic body: the messages, a model from an allowed set, and max tokens with an upper bound. Bad input is a 422 before anything costs money.
Then two dependencies. Get current user verifies the JWT. Check budget reads the user's token count in Redis, and replies 429 when it's spent.
If it's retrieval augmented, retrieval runs as async calls to the vector store, with their own timeout. Any CPU-heavy step, like local re-ranking, goes off the event loop.
The model call uses one async client created in the lifespan, a semaphore to stay under the provider's limit, a timeout, and retries with backoff on transient errors only.
The answer streams back as server sent events, stopping if the client disconnects. After the stream, record the actual token usage and save the conversation, tagged with the request id.

And around it: provider overloaded becomes 503 with retry after; a timeout becomes 504. Observe time to first token, p95 latency, tokens and cost. Scale with more workers or pods, keeping nothing per user in process memory. Every module of this lecture, in one endpoint.
Compressed into an answer you can say in forty seconds.
An async def POST chat route with a bounded Pydantic body, and JWT auth and a token budget as dependencies.
Shared async clients created in the lifespan, with a semaphore, timeouts, and retries on transient errors only.
Retrieval with its own timeout, and any CPU work kept off the event loop.
Tokens streamed with server sent events, stopping on disconnect, and usage recorded at the end.
Provider errors mapped cleanly to 503 and 504; time to first token, p95, tokens and cost observed; and stateless workers that scale out. Then the interviewer picks a layer, and you go deeper.
